| D106 | **Timers in a script** (amends D76, D79, D87; P8, P16, D64, D77, D81, D85): a script woke only on an event, so one that should act once a day, or each minute, needed an event to ride on, or a module of its own. **Now** the script API has `at(time, fn)` (`time` in ms since the epoch or a `Date`; one past fires as soon as it can) and `every(ms, fn)` (on each whole multiple of `ms` since the epoch, so `every(60_000, fn)` fires at second :00 of each minute), each giving a handle with `cancel()`, and both callable at any time, in its first run or in a handler (unlike `on`). **On its node's clock:** the runtime keeps each timer's function, and the host arms it on `ctx.clock`, in the main thread, whichever the isolation; in a worker, the runtime asks for it by a message and hears it due by a message, as it hears an event, so the worker holds no timer of its own and stays idle, unpinged, until then (D87). The host re-arms a beat of `every` itself, before it fires, for the next multiple after the time it was due or now, whichever is later: a leap of the dev kit's virtual clock fires each beat on the way, at its own time, and a beat missed while the host stalled is not made up for. A wait longer than a timer holds (about 24.8 days) is armed again on the way. **A fire is a call like a handler's:** under the same limits (vm's `callMs` in process, the watchdog's CPU limit in a worker, D81, D85), counted in its cost (D77, D87), its error logged (`a timer threw: …`) with the script going on, its hang failing its node (`its script hung: a timer of every(60000) spent over 1000 ms of CPU`). **Limits:** an interval of 1000 ms at least, and 100 timers pending at most per script; past either, the call throws, with why. **In memory only:** its node's stop, its stop by exception (`pause`, D64), its failure, a restart or a reload drops them all, and a script that starts again runs from the top; so a script sets its timers in its first run, and keeps in its `store` what it must remember (the day its daily action was last done), catching up at start what it missed while down. A script exported as a plugin (D79) gets the same two on `ctx.clock`, armed at its start and dropped at its stop, without the limits. **Its cost:** in a worker on the dev kit's clock, a timer set during a leap (from a timer's run) is armed once its message arrives, after the leap; a test that needs it exact runs in process. Rejected: durable timers (`ctx.scheduler`), which a script that runs from the top at each start would set again each time; timers in the worker, on a clock of its own, which the dev kit's virtual clock would not drive; and `setTimeout`/`setInterval` by their names, which read as real time and invite many short ones. | D107 | **A command no answer came for is told; a declaration names only the commands that draw it** (amends D98; P5, P6, D91, D93; #59): a game ignored a command in one chat without a word (a game's purchase sent in the private chat with its bot, which it takes only in its group). Its send waited its window and settled `unanswered`, which only an `await enqueue(…)` heard: the watchdog (D93) counts it, but any event read from the chat starts its counts again, so with the bot answering other commands there it never stops the node, and the owner learnt nothing. Worse, while it waited, a refusal of another command whose declaration also named it (one rule for every command of a group) was paired with it, as the oldest send waiting, and three such refusals made the retry-loop guard hold back a command the bot had never refused. **Told:** a send whose window ends unanswered raises an `unanswered` notice about each node it went for (`detail`: `account`, `chat`, `command`, `withinS`; told by `owner-notice` among its `other` kinds), **once** until a send of that command by that node to that chat is answered, so that a script sending it every minute raises one, and a bot that answers again re-arms it. **Paired as before:** the core still pairs an answer with the send it replies to, else the oldest waiting send of its declared commands. It cannot tell which of those commands a message answers, so **a declaration names only the commands that can draw its event**, which is the parser's contract, not a hint; a parser reading several chats where its bot answers some commands in only some of them marks the payload (a field of its own) and declares those commands `unless` it. **Its cost:** a slow bot (an answer after its window) raises one notice; the owner may confirm the threshold (first unanswered send, not the third as the guard). within two seconds); refusing a command at send time in a chat its bot ignores it in (the core knows no chat's kind, and the parser's declaration would have to name chats, D49) (bot-os-api.md §4.6, | D108 | **A queued send waits for its account to connect** (amends D73; P5, P8, D64, D95, D98): a script that queued a send as soon as it ran (a timer at its first run, D106) had it refused `not connected`, its `cancel` deadline of half an hour notwithstanding, because the account's Telegram connector was still connecting at the instance's start; the queue, which waits out intervals, rates and cooldowns, did not wait for the one thing that was sure to come. **Now** the core tells each outbox where its account's connection is: `connected`; `connecting`, a connector of the account about to start, starting, or running and (re)connecting (its status `connecting`, as at the start or after a drop); `down`, no connector running (none, stopped, disabled, inactive, failed). | D109 | **No edge, no chat command: a command is served through the graph** (amends D29, D56, D63, P11; P6, P10, P17, D64, D94, D96, D100; amended by D110, D167): a plugin declared its chat commands (`interface.commands`), the core listed every running plugin's, and every connector offering a chat surface (a `telegram-bot` with its `owner`) registered and answered them all, in its group, the owner's chat and any private chat, to anyone (but a handler's `allow` or the bot's `deny`), replying outside the plugin's outbox: a node answered `/map` in the owner's public group with no edge touching any connector. The owner: _"The graph should be self-evident. Our UI isn't simply a way to perform some configuration changes; its main goal is to spot the architecture at a glance. Something as important as a command must be represented in the graph."_ It broke P17 (the edges are the permissions: which module talks to which), P10 (what a plugin sends is held by the shell: node states, dry runs) and the spirit of D94 (no hidden behaviour on live channels); D29's _an answer is like a web page_ holds for the admin side (the web UI, the control API), not for a public group or a stranger's private chat. **A port type, `commands`.** A plugin that declares commands has a **`commands` input, derived** from its manifest (as a connector's chat-out input is from its account: the commands are declared once, in `interface.commands`; a port declared under that name is refused), optional (no edge: it runs, and no chat asks it anything). A connector that can serve commands **declares a `commands` output** (`outputs: { commands: { type: 'commands' } }`, of its account's network; only a connector may): today `telegram-bot`, which serves them only with its `owner` set (its chat surface); any connector may, by declaring it and offering a `ChatSurface`. **The edge** runs from the connector's output to the plugin's input, either end taking any number (one edge per connector and plugin), and carries: `serves`, the commands it serves (by name, its plugin's; none: all); `chats`, the chats it answers in, as edges name chats (`Surface.id`, picked in the chat picker, D96, never typed) and `privateChats`, every private chat with the account too; `senders`, who may ask (none: anyone; a list of `@username`s or ids, `owner` for the connector's owner), the plugin's `allow(asker)` still applying on top, and the bot's `deny` (D100) before it; `dryRun`. The check refuses a command its plugin does not declare, and these fields on another edge (and `reads` on it); it warns of an edge that names no chat (answered nowhere). **The surface** (`ChatSurface.serve`) is given `core.served(node)`: the commands its edges serve, each with where (`ChatCommand.where`, `inScope`), and registers each in the menus of the chats it is served in alone (the owner's chat and the group through the switchboard, every private chat's menu, Telegram's `chat` scope for another chat named), and answers it there alone; a command asked anywhere else is neither listed nor answered, and `Request.chat` tells the handler the chat. `core.commands()` still lists every plugin's, for the admin side, which reaches them all. **Replies are held by the shell:** a node disabled, stopped or inactive answers nothing (as before, its handler not run); each answer, text or photo, is recorded as a send (`core.send`, its origin `command /<name>`, the chat, `live` or `dry-run`, `sent` or `failed` with why), so that the events panel shows it and the owner's summary counts it; a **dry-run** edge logs the answer it would have sent and sends nothing, and a new edge starts a dry run (P10). D29's point stays within the edge: the answer goes to the asker, in the chat asked. **The owner's controls stay as they are** (`/plugins`, `/kill`, `/settings`, `/set`, their cards and buttons, D56): the core's own, not a plugin's, answered to the owner alone in the owner's chat, which is in the graph already as the bot's `owner` config, the instance's control surface rather than a plugin's channel; a plugin's command marked `owner: true` needs an edge as any other (the edge cannot widen it: it stays the owner's, in the owner's chat). **Migration** (removed by D110; `commandEdges` ran once per instance): at the first start of this release, a saved graph gets, from each connector node whose commands output says what it served before (`servedBefore: { when, chats, privateChats }`: `telegram-bot`'s `{ when: 'owner', chats: ['owner', 'group'], privateChats: true }`) and whose config sets `when`, an edge to each node with commands not joined to it already: every command, in its owner's chat, its group and every private chat, to anyone, **live**, so nothing changes; the file is written as a version of the history (`migrated`), recorded (`core.graph`, `commandEdges`) and the owner told which edges were added (a `graph-migrated` notice). An edge the owner removes afterwards stays removed; a fresh instance adds none. **The editor** draws the port (its own colour and shape), accepts a drag from a connector's commands output to a plugin's commands input and no other (D101's `bindProblem`, by type), and starts a new edge a dry run in the connector's owner's chat; the edge's panel has the commands as checkboxes, the chats in the chat picker, a box for every private chat, the senders (anyone, or a list with _the owner_) and the dry run; a plugin's panel says, for each command, which connector serves it, in which chats by name and to whom, or that no edge does (and its card's `commands` port says so too), a connector's which plugins' commands it serves; an edge's rhombus tells it in words, hollow while a dry run. The chat-in edges' and chat-out edges' lists stay distinct: a chat-out's `commands` are the first words a plugin may send; a commands edge's `serves`, the chat commands it answers. **Module authors change nothing:** a plugin declaring commands keeps its manifest and handlers; it is served once an edge reaches it (migrated, or drawn). A connector of a module that wants to serve commands declares a `commands` output. **Its cost:** a new plugin with commands answers nobody until the owner draws its edge and sends it for real; a person's chat named by `@username` gets no menu of its own (Telegram takes a chat's menu by id), though answered. Rejected: a declared commands input (a second place to name the commands); answering every chat of a bot from one edge with no chat list (the hidden default this removes); folding the commands into chat-in edges' `senders` and `commands` (a chat-in carries what a parser reads, not what a plugin answers); edges for the owner's own controls (the owner's chat is already the connector's config) (bot-os-api.md §2, §2.1, §2.3, §4.5, §4.8, §4.11, §4.16) the outbox's `Mode` is now `SendMode`, `dry-run` or `live`); the conversions a saved graph went through as it loaded (`upgradeGraph`, `Core.upgrade`, `GraphChecker.upgrade`: version 1's chat edges split, D60; | D111 | **What belongs to a node is shown on it: the Admin page's features move into the editor** (amends D47, D55, D59, D61, D77; P16, P17, D109; #53): the graph editor is the main UI (D55), yet the Admin page (D59) still held most of what the owner reads and does to a node, in tables of their own: a plugin's state, its status, settings, reads and actions (Plugins), a connector's account and connection (Accounts), what each node costs (Resources), next to the instance's switches and health (Instance) and the graph's history and printout. D109's principle holds for the UI as a whole: _the graph should be self-evident; its main goal is to spot the architecture at a glance_; what belongs to a node is shown on that node, and a page apart is left for what has none. **Into the node's panel:** a connector's account as it runs, as whom, and its connection's state and step (`GET /accounts`); what the node costs since the start, its share of the whole and whether it is among the top three (D77); and, while it runs, its own status (its `status` read, shown in its Status section and so offered no Read button among its reads), its settings **in force**, each set at once as `/set` does in chat (`POST /settings`), above the settings form of the draft (what a fresh instance starts with), and its reads and actions, each called from the panel, its input filled in a form made from its schema rather than typed as JSON, its answer or its refusal shown under it. Its state, its stop (source, time, reason, Clear stop), its kill and its kinds were in the panel already: the Admin copies go. **On the node's cards:** a connector's connection (`connected`, `connecting`, `closed`, its step on hover), so that an account down is seen on the map. **On the map's bar:** the instance's switches, always there: `instance on` or `off`, **Turn off** (asking first) or **Turn on**, and **Kill all** (every plugin's safety stop, asking first, D30, D44). **In the bottom bar,** on every page: the instance's health beside its release, how long it has run and its memory (its Node version and heap on hover), read every minute. The plugins and accounts counted by state go: each node's state is on its card. **Side sheets of the editor:** the costs' table (sortable, the top three marked) is the **Costs** tab under the Text tab, each node's name selecting it; the saved graph printed (Admin's Graph as text) goes, the Text tab's draft printed being the same graph while nothing is changed, and the history showing any version's. **The Admin page keeps what has no node:** the graph's history and its rollback (D61), and is named after it, **History** (its tab and its heading; its route still `#/admin`, `#/graph-history` still leading to it); the events and the drift reports stay pages of their own. **Old routes** still lead somewhere: `#/graph-history` to Admin, scrolled to it; `#/instance`, `#/accounts` and `#/plugins` to the editor; `#/resources` and `#/graph-text` to the editor with the Costs or the Text sheet open. No numeric id is shown: an account by its `<network>:<name>` and the name it runs as. The control API is unchanged (bot-os-api.md §4.11). Rejected: keeping the Plugins and Accounts tables beside the panels (two places for one thing, one of them out of the graph); a node's live settings in a form made from its settings schema (each keystroke would set one at once; a value is set with its own Set) | D112 | **A node's widget and page, declared from its reads** (P11, P16, P17, D11, D49, D111; #50; amended by D134, D169, D170, D172): P16 promised pages contributed by plugins, "widgets with a plugin's own status on the dashboard, and full pages where a plugin has more to show", and D11 a web UI with plugin widgets; neither was built, and since D111 the dashboard is the graph editor, where what belongs to a node is shown on it. **Per node:** a widget belongs to a node, not to its plugin: two nodes of one plugin show two, each its own instance's. **Declared, not coded:** a plugin's manifest may declare a `widget`, one section, and a `page`, `{ title, sections }`; a section names one of its reads (`interface.state`, P11), the read's `input` if it takes one, a dotted `path` into its output, an optional `label` (else the output schema's description there, else the path's last key), and how it shows the value (`show`), one of six: `keyValue` (fields, the named ones or every key), `counter` (a number, or a list's or a map's size), `list` (items, by an `item` path, at most `max`), `table` (rows, a column per `columns` path, at most `max`), `progress` (an amount out of `of`, a number or a path) and `until` (a time, ms or ISO, as how long until it or since). The web UI draws them generically (`Widget.tsx`), knowing no plugin, so no game code enters the shell (D49), and a module adds a widget by declaring it. They are **checked as the rest of the manifest:** a read not declared, an input its schema refuses, a path its output's schema has not (one into a value its schema leaves open stands), or a value of a kind the section cannot show is refused at load, by its field (`widget.path: the read status has no silver`). **On the card, a line:** the editor's purpose is to see the architecture at a glance (D109), so a widget is one line in its node's head, cut short and whole on hover (`Gold: 40 · Who: alice`, `12 Items`, `Next turn: in 12m 5s`, a bar for a progress), drawn while the node runs; its card is a line taller whenever its plugin declares one, so that the map does not move as nodes start and stop. **The page** is reached from the node's panel (**Open its page**, while it runs), at `#/node/<id>`, in no menu, its sections drawn in full (a list of terms, a big number, a list, a table, a bar, a time with its UTC). **Refresh:** the card's value comes with `GET /status` (`widget`: the output of the read the widget names, read by the core for each running node; its `status` read reused when it is the same; left out while the read throws), which the editor asks every five seconds already, so a widget costs no request of its own; the page asks each of its reads once (however many sections show it) every five seconds while open (since D172, while its browser tab is visible, never twice at once); an `until` moves every second on its own. **First user:** the turn actor: its next turn on its card, and a page, Turns, with its chat, its command, its last and its next turn; the game modules' stats and ledgers follow in their own repositories. **Not for scripts:** a script node offers no reads (its code runs in a worker thread, which a read, synchronous, cannot ask), so it declares no widget; giving scripts reads would come first. Rejected: a widget as a component a module ships (code of a module in the UI's bundle, against D49 and the UI's imports, bot-os-api.md §6); a widget per plugin (two nodes, one widget: the wrong one for one of them); a refresh rate per widget (one cadence, the status's, until a widget needs another); widgets listed on the Admin page (D111 moved what belongs to a node onto it) (bot-os-api.md §2, Widgets and pages, §4.11, §4.12, §5) | D113 | **Drift reports by the parser's version** (amended by D166; P5, P16, D7; amends nothing): the Drift page listed a parser's latest reports over a week from the event log, so after its module was upgraded (applied with a restart, which resets the counts in memory) the old version's unread messages lingered, read as if the new one still failed them. **Each `core.drift` record carries the `version` the parser runs**, its module's as loaded (`GET /modules`), or the release's for one of the image's own (`GET /instance`); `GET /status` gives each node's `version` the same way, which is where the page reads it (one field on a call it can make, rather than a parser listed by `GET /drift` before it has reported). **The page shows, per parser, the reports of the version it runs**, and folds the others under one line, `N from earlier versions`, that opens them. | D115 | **A tool in the image creates a `telegram-user` session string** (P9, D18, D49; #55): a `telegram-user` connector needs a session string as a Docker secret, and nothing in the image made one: `login()` was there, run by no command since v0's CLI went. **The tool:** `packages/connectors/tools/telegram-login.ts`, run in the image (`docker run -it --rm <image> node packages/connectors/tools/telegram-login.ts`), asks for the API id and hash (my.telegram.org), the phone number, the code Telegram sends and the 2FA password if set (the hash and the password not echoed), checks the pair as the plugin does (`apiProblems`), logs in with `login()` and prints the session string to save as `telegram_user_session`, beside `telegram_user_api_id` and `telegram_user_api_hash`. | D116 | **A Telegram connector logs in from its node** (amends P9, D10, D18; P11, P16, D55, D63, D111; #11): a Telegram connection was set up outside the app, a bot's token and an account's API pair and session as Docker secrets, the session printed by a command (D115). **Where credentials live:** a connector whose manifest says `login` keeps them in its own store (`login.json`, mode 600, in the volume), from a login in its node's panel; at `create` it reads them **before** its Docker secrets, which stay a fallback and are no longer required at the load (amended by D118: no Docker secret any more, the store alone). **Needs login:** a connector with neither runs anyway, as `LoginNeeded` (closed, phase `needs login`, on its card), so a new one is added, applied, logged in, restarted and its chats ticked (D63 lists them once it connects). **The login, generic:** its instance offers `login`, `{ state(), act(action, values) }`; its state says what it asks next (a step's title, how-to, link, QR code, fields, secret ones unseen) and the buttons offered; the web UI draws it in the node's panel knowing no network, as it draws forms from schemas (P11), and asks again every 2 s while a login is under way. The control API serves it, behind the web UI's login like the rest (`GET` and `POST /plugins/<id>/login`, bot-os-api.md §4.11). **Logged in, restart:** the credentials are put in force by a restart (the panel's **Restart now**, as Apply's), not in place: a connector is made from them at `create` and its bot or client is shared by its surface and its queue; no node restarts alone (D16). **telegram-bot:** the @BotFather token, pasted, checked with `getMe` ("as @ExampleBot") before it is kept; **Forget the token** drops it (revoking it is @BotFather's `/revoke`). **telegram-user:** the API id and hash, entered once (my.telegram.org, with a how-to: the project cannot ship its own pair, which would be abused and banned), then a login **by QR code** first (GramJS 2.26.22's `signInUserWithQrCode`: the page shows the `tg://login` link as a QR code, renewed as it expires, to scan in Telegram's Settings → Devices → Link Desktop Device), or **by phone** (the number, the code, the 2FA password); a wrong code or password is asked again; one login at a time, held open for GramJS's callbacks and dropped after 5 minutes without an answer; its session shows in the account's Devices as the app registered at my.telegram.org on a device named `MegaBotTron1999`, revocable from the phone; **Log out** ends it on Telegram's side too (`auth.logOut`) and keeps the API pair. **Secrets in the logs:** each value typed (but a code, too short to redact) and each credential kept is marked secret (`ctx.secrets.remember`), so the core redacts it from what it prints, records and answers; each action is recorded (`core.login`: node, action, outcome, whom as), never a value. **Accepted:** the credentials sit in the volume and its backups in clear, as the secrets' directory would; no encryption at rest, its key beside them (amends P9; the core's `secretStore` under `bot_os_key` stays for the core's own; amended by D123: sealed under `bot_os_key`). Rejected: a token checked in the draft before its node runs (the check needs a running connector; a draft has none); a connector rebuilt in place after a login (its bot or client is shared, and D16 has no hot reload); a QR code drawn on the server (the page draws it, with `qrcode-generator`, the web UI's build dependency, MIT, no dependencies of its own) | D117 | **A model connector: a `$` on its node, every call's cost logged, the last 24 hours on it** (P5, P6, P11, P16, D49, D52, D77, D112; #27): a connector to a model (today `anthropic`) spends the owner's money on each call, so it is told apart and watched. **Marked by its manifest:** `model: true` (only a connector), rather than a kind of its own, which would change what the kinds mean (what a node does, not what it costs); so another model connector gets the same treatment by saying so. The editor draws a `$` on its card (`GET /available`'s `model`). **Every call logged by the connector,** not left to its callers, which could forget: the core tells an action who calls it (`ActionCall`, its second argument: `{ node }`, the node whose interface input the call came through, which the caller cannot pass or forge; none for the owner's controls), and the connector writes one record per call, `<plugin>.call`: the calling node (`(owner)` for the panel), the model, `ok` (and `error`), its input, output, cache-write and cache-read tokens, and its cost in `usd`, never the prompt or the answer. **Prices** are a table in the connector's code (`PRICES`), not its config, so that a release updates them and no saved config freezes an old table (the editor writes a config's defaults into it): USD per million tokens by model id (input, output, 5-minute and 1-hour cache writes, cache reads, and `over`, dearer prices for a prompt over so many tokens, as Claude Haiku 5.5's over 100K), Anthropic's published pricing for its own API on 2026-11-03, every current Claude model the connector can be configured with, the cache reads it does not publish per model derived from its rule of about a tenth of the input and marked so; a config saved with the `prices` key it once had still loads, its schema dropping the key; a dated snapshot (`<id>-20251001`) takes its id's price. A model with none is **not guessed:** its calls are logged with `usd: null` and counted as unpriced, and the connector warns once a run, naming it. **The last 24 hours** are kept in the connector's store (`spend`), by the hour, by calling node and by model, written at each call (one small document, a call to a model being seconds and cents), so the figure survives a restart at no cost: no read of the event log at start. The window is the hours that overlap the last 24, so up to 25 hours of calls. **Shown through D112, with no code of its own in the shell:** its `status` read (the totals, a cost in words, `byNode` and `byModel`) is its widget, `Last 24 h — Cost: $0.42 · Calls: 14` on its card, its panel's Status section, which breaks it down by calling node, and its page, Spend, a table by node and one by model; its `Instance.cost` gives the D77 costs its `spend` (`usd`, `calls`, `unpriced`), a column of the Costs sheet and a line of its panel's Cost. Rejected: a `model` kind; prices in the config (frozen in each saved node); a record left to each caller (a script would not); rebuilding the 24 hours from the event log at start (a day's files read for one figure); guessing an unknown model's price from its family. Not counted: fast mode, batches and partner platforms' prices, which the connector does not use | D118 | **The Telegram connectors take no Docker secret** (amends D116, supersedes D115; P9, P11, D49): D116 kept the secrets (`telegram_bot_token`, `telegram_user_api_id`, `telegram_user_api_hash`, `telegram_user_session`) as a fallback beside the login from the node, and D115 shipped a tool whose only use was to print a session for that secret; so a Telegram connector had two ways in, the panel said which one it ran on ("from its Docker secrets", **Log in here instead**, a fallback on logout), and an owner setting one up met both. **Now** `telegram-bot` and `telegram-user` declare no secret: their credentials live only in their store, from the login in their node's panel; without them they run as `LoginNeeded`. Other connectors' secrets (`znc_password`, `anthropic_api_key`, a `configSecrets` key's) are unchanged. | D123 | **A connector's credentials sealed at rest** (amends P9, D116; D10, D18, D118): D116 accepted the credentials a login keeps (a bot's token, an account's API pair and session) in the connector's store in clear, and D118 left the store their only place; so the volume and every backup of it held a token and a session that give full access. **Now** a connector keeps them through `ctx.secrets.store`, a view of its own store whose documents are sealed (`Sealer`: AES-256-GCM, its key derived by HKDF-SHA256 from the `bot_os_key` Docker secret, the instance and document's name as additional data, the IV an HMAC of those and the value, so that one value seals the same way, as SIV does), opened in memory only, every string opened remembered for redaction. Generic: any connector, the Telegram ones first. **Without the key** they are written in clear (mode 600), so that a fresh install still logs in, and the node says so (its login's `atRest: "clear"`, a warning in its panel: provide the key); refusing to keep them would leave a fresh install unable to log in at all. With it, `atRest: "sealed"`; a document kept in clear before is sealed as soon as it is read with the key, at the next start. **A changed or missing key:** a sealed document that does not open reads as none, so the connector runs needing a login, its login's error saying why, until it logs in again; nothing crashes. Rejected: a random IV (a value sealed twice would differ, so a document or a graph written again unchanged would seem changed); encryption in each connector (one mechanism, the core's); a key stored in the volume (it would sit beside what it seals) | D124 | **A plugin marks sensitive config fields: sealed in the graph's file, never shown back** (P9, P11, D50, D55, D61, D75, D123): a value typed into a node's config (an API key, a password) sat in `graph.json` and its history in clear, and every view of a graph (its JSON, its text, the check, the history's versions and line diffs) printed it; only the Docker secrets' redaction, by value, stood between it and the page. **The mark:** the manifest's `configSensitive`, the keys of its config, beside `configSecrets` and `configChats`, any kind of plugin; rather than a schema annotation, which zod's JSON Schema would carry to the page but not to the core's file handling as plainly. **At rest:** a sensitive value is sealed in the graph's file and in each version of its history (the `Sealer` of D123, under `bot_os_key`, its config key as additional data, so a node renamed keeps it; the same value seals the same way, so a graph written again unchanged is the same graph), opened in memory for the running node and the check. **Shown nowhere:** one function, `hideSensitive`, turns every sensitive value, clear, sealed or hidden, into `{ "$sensitive": "set" }`, and every path by which a graph leaves the core goes through it: `GET /graph/file`, `GET /graph`, `/graph/view` and its node views, `POST /graph/check`'s diff and text, the history's versions, texts and line diffs, a rollback, the audit records of a save; `graphText` prints any such form as `[sensitive]`; and each value opened is remembered as a secret, redacted from logs, records, errors and notices. **The editor** says set or not set, and offers **Replace** (typed unseen) and **Clear**; it sends `{ "$sensitive": "set" }` back for a value left as it was, which the core takes from the saved file by node id and key. **Existing graphs:** a value in clear is sealed at the next save, not at the load (the load writes nothing); a history version that holds one in clear keeps it until it ages out (7 days, 5 versions), shown hidden meanwhile, and restoring it writes it sealed. **No key:** written as typed, as the file always was. **A missing or changed key:** a value that does not open is left out of the node's config, with a warning from the check and the load (`its sealed value does not open`): the node runs without it or fails as its schema says, and the owner sets it again; nothing crashes. No first-party plugin marks a key today: their credentials are Docker secrets (`configSecrets`) or logins (D123). Rejected: sealing at the load (the load would rewrite the owner's file and its history behind their back); a random IV (every save a change) | D125 | **A connector waiting for its login does not fail the health, and a stopped one still logs in** (amends D116, D122; P16; amended by D143): a connector set up by login only (D118) starts with none, so the health endpoint answered 503 until it was logged in; a proxy that leaves unhealthy containers out (Traefik does) then took the web UI away, the only place it logs in from. | D126 | **A phone login's code can be resent** (amends D116; P16): a `telegram-user` login by phone asked for the code Telegram sent, and Telegram often sends it to the account's app (`SentCodeTypeApp`: a message from its official "Telegram" chat, on a device already logged in), where an owner may never see it, with no way but to cancel. **Now** the code step offers **Resend the code**: the open code question is refused with `RESTART_AUTH`, on which GramJS's `signInUser` starts again; its new run is given the same number at once, its parameters now with `forceSMS`, so that GramJS sends a new code (`auth.SendCode`) and, unless that went by SMS, asks for the next way (`auth.ResendCode`: an SMS or a call, as Telegram offers). twice) | D127 | **A config's choice drawn as labelled radio buttons, and fields shown for a choice** (amends D55; P11, P16): a config that sets a mode, then a list that applies only in that mode (`telegram-bot`'s groups and people, D128), drew the mode as a bare select of its values (`any`, `only`) and every list at once, those of the mode not chosen included, whose values would hold unseen. Two keys a plugin may put on a config field's schema, through zod's `.meta()`, which the core's JSON Schema carries as it carries `description`: **`choices: { <value>: '<label>' }`** on an enum, drawn as one radio button per value, each by its label (`Any group it is added to`), the value kept as before; **`shownWhen: { <key>: <value> }`** on any field, drawn only while each sibling key named has that value (an unset one at its default), and taken away from the config by the change that makes it not apply, so that a list of the mode left never lingers hidden (switching back starts it empty). Both are generic (`SchemaForm.tsx`), a chat picker's key (D96) included, and read by the form alone: the config's own check still says what a value of the wrong mode means (`telegram-bot`'s refuses it). Rejected: a select of the raw values, which tells the owner nothing; hiding a field yet keeping its value, which leaves the config doing what the form does not show; a nested object per mode (`groups: { mode, only, block }`), which the chat picker's keys (`configChats`, top-level keys) cannot reach. | D128 | **Where and for whom a bot works: groups and people, each any or only these** (replaces D100; amends D56, D96, D109; P4, P11, P16, D127; amended by D160): a `telegram-bot` had an owner, one optional `group` ("whose members may use the plugins' public commands": the switchboard's second topic, its menu and its throttles, and a role in the chats it lists), and a `deny` list of people whose commands in a group it dropped. The owner's model is wider: **who it works for, as allow or block, for groups and for people**; and `group`, a single radio that could not be unset, named one group among the many a bot is in. **Its config** (flat keys, so that the chat picker reaches each list, `configChats` naming top-level keys): `groups`, `any` (default, "Any group it is added to") or `only` ("Only these groups"), then `onlyGroups` for `only`, or, for `any`, an optional `blockGroups` ("groups it ignores all the same"); `people`, `anyone` (default) or `only`, then `onlyPeople`, or for `anyone` an optional `blockPeople` (D100's `deny`); `denyReply` kept. The form draws each choice as labelled radios and shows only the list of the choice made (D127); the check refuses a list of the choice not made (`set only with groups: only`), so a chat can never be both allowed and blocked, and refuses the owner in `blockPeople`. **Its owner always works**: allowed whether `onlyPeople` lists them or not, which its help says rather than refusing. **The gate, the connector's outer check** (`telegram-gate.ts`, first in the bot's chain, before any chat-in edge, commands edge or the surface): in a group it does not work in, **nothing goes further**, neither a command (recorded) nor a message (to no reader): a group it does not work in is one it is not in, for every plugin, and `chats` (what it monitors) only narrows within the groups it works in. A **person** it does not work for has their **commands and taps dropped, in any chat**, a group's or a private one (D100 spared private chats; "who it works for" is the person's, wherever they ask), but **what they say still reaches the readers**: a module may read another bot's messages that no one lets command it, and an `only` list of people would otherwise blind it. Each command dropped is recorded as before (`telegram-bot.denied`, now with `by`: `group` or `person`) and counted on its node; `denyReply` answers a person, never a group it does not work in. **The menus and the throttles:** `group` went, and so did the switchboard's group topic: every group is answered through the Bot API, with a group's throttles (one per user a minute, one every 10 s) each group its own (a group no config named had a private chat's before) and `deleteInGroupAfterMs` in any group; each chat a commands edge names gets its menu in Telegram's `chat` scope, retried until set and set again when the bot joins it (the group's topic had that alone), but a group the gate refuses. Not Telegram's `all_group_chats` scope for `any`: a command is answered only in the chats its edge names (D109), so a menu in every group would list commands that none answers. **Commands edges** keep their `chats`, `privateChats` and `senders`, the inner, per-plugin narrowing within what the gate lets in. Rejected: a nested object per dimension (`groups: { mode, only, block }`), out of `configChats`' reach; allow and block lists side by side, whose overlap needs a precedence rule; gating what people say (it would blind modules reading other bots); keeping `group` for the menu (any group an edge names now has one) (bot-os-api.md §4.5, §4.11) | D129 | **A turn is a turn: the owner's last turn counts the group's too** (amends D99; amended by D134): a turn parser's `state.lastTurn`, from which its actor counts, kept only the owner's turns in the private chat with its bot, though it reads the owner's turns in the game's group as well and their answers set the bot's rest. | D131 | **A recorded chat, replayed through real plugins** (P15, D130; #60, #49): replay tools called a parser's read functions directly, bypassing its chat-in port, its store, the clock, rests, turns and answers, so what they checked was not what runs. **Now** the dev kit replays: `replay` (in `@megabottron1999/telegram-export`) takes a module's plugins, or a graph file in the live format, and the `Inbound`s of an export (D130), swaps each `telegram-user` node for a `FakeConnector` of the same id, configuration (the real plugin's schema) and account, which delivers only the chats its `chats` lists, named as listed, as live, and feeds the messages in time order on the kit's `VirtualClock`: the clock runs to each message's time first, every timer due on the way at its own time, so rests, timers and answers behave as live; live, or all as history (`playback`). | D132 | **Each command's readiness, in the turn-parser contract** (amended by D141, D142, D165; amends D70, D98; P5, D49, D62, D83, D99, D129; #61): a turn parser knew one thing of when its bot may be played, its rest after a turn (`state.rest`), and the turn actor one command; but games offer more than a turn: a command usable once a day, one unlocked by an announcement in an answer, one that resets another command's wait, which a person takes as they come. **Declared by the game, as data, additively:** a `TurnParserSpec` may name the bot's other commands (`commands`, by first word, never a turn command) with their mechanics in generic terms: a **cooldown** (`cooldownMin`: held that long after a success), an **announced unlock** (`unlock`: held from the start and after each success until a message of the bot, in private or answering the owner, matches its `pattern`, a regular expression on the text, or a reading names it in `unlocks`; for `forMin` minutes if given) and **effects** (`effects`: at its success, another command's hold ended, `clear`, a reset, or shortened, `shortenMin`; a turn command's is the rest they share). A reading may say what any message announces (`unlocks`, `effects`), so a grammar can drive both from what the bot writes. **Tracked by the parser:** it knows the sends of those commands as it knows the turns (by hand, or told by `actions.sent`, which takes a `command`, a turn when none), matches their answers the same way, tells the grammar which command a message answers (`BotMessage.command`), publishes them as `<id>.answer` (`{ chat, command, outcome, retryAt?, holds?, playback? }`; the turn's stay `<id>.turn`), and keeps each command's state in its store (`parsed.commands`). **Exposed** as a new read, `state.ready`: by command, `{ ready, since?, until?, why?, sent?, answer? }`, ready since when or held until when (none: until an unlock) and why, its last send with whether by hand, and the last answer read to it with its length; a turn command's derives from the rest, unchanged, and `rest` and `lastTurn` stay as they were (`lastTurn` counts turn commands only). A "too soon" (`nothing`/`cooldown`) holds a command for the wait it says and is no success. **The outbox follows** (D98): each other command is answered by its `<id>.answer` (`when: { command }`, so its cooldown holds it alone), and an answer declaration may name `holdsAtFrom`, a path to a map of times by command set as it says, an earlier time too, one past clearing it: the effects' holds go in the event (`holds`), so a reset ends the outbox's cooldown on the turn as well as the parser's rest, where `retryAtFrom` keeps the latest. A spec without `commands` reads, publishes and declares exactly what it did. Rejected: a grammar's code tracking readiness (each game would re-implement the same holds; data the shell reads keeps D49); readiness per node config (which commands unlock or reset is the game's fact, as D70 says of turns); replacing `rest` with `ready` (the contract is additive, so existing grammars and their tests stand); the reset left to the parser alone (the outbox would still refuse the turn it allows, holding the latest `retryAt`) (bot-os-api.md §4.6, §5) | D133 | **The `attention` port: a simulated person, many players** (P6, P17, D27, D64; #61): each turn actor carried its own pace (gaps, skip chance, nights off), so the bots a person plays ran on independent clocks, and nothing tied them to one person. A person sits down, plays what is ready, and leaves; whatever they play then shares that sitting. **A sixth port type, `attention`**, declared both ways: an output `{ type: 'attention' }` on the node that holds a person's attention, which any number of edges leave (players attached to one person share their sittings), and an input `{ type: 'attention', optional?, bind? }` on each node that plays, one edge (`bound twice` otherwise), required unless optional: so the person starts first, and a person disabled or stopped makes its players inactive (D64), as a parser does its actor. It **carries nothing**: no chats, no members; the check refuses a chat-out's or a commands edge's fields on it as on any other edge. **At runtime** the core hands the player what the person's node offers it: the person's instance returns `attention: (node) => …`, which `ctx.attention(port?)` calls with the asking node's id (`attention` by default; refused for an input it does not have, unbound, or whose person is not running); what they exchange is the two plugins' agreement, as an interface's members are, so the core knows no person and no game. Drawn as its type is (`PORT_TYPE_INFO`: a square, dark amber), in the editor's legend with the others; the editor draws and checks it generically. | D134 | **`attention` and the `player`, in place of the turn actor** (amended by D141; replaces the turn actor; amends D99, D112, D129; P3, P5, P10, P17, D64, D92, D97, D98, D132, D133; #61): each turn actor carried its own schedule (gaps, skip chance, nights off), repeated on each turn node, and sent one command at random intervals; a person plays in sittings: they play a turn, read the answer, take whatever just unlocked, and leave until they next come back. **`attention`**, a native plugin, one node per person (or account), holds once what every turn actor held (`minGapMin`, `maxGapMin`, `skipChance`, the nights, `timeZone`, `seed`; the planner moved to `sittings.ts`, its nights now always drawn from their date and the node's id, so a restart keeps them; the floor of 15 minutes on the gap, the bots' rest, gone with it: the parsers' readiness guards the rest now, the gap is the person's, 1 minute at least) and the person's reaction time within a sitting (`reaction`: a glance of `minS`–`maxS` seconds, `perCharMs` more per character of the answer read, `readMaxS` seconds at most (D146), and with `longChance` up to `longMaxS` more). It starts **sittings** through its `attention` output (D133), every player at once, so the players of one person share them; and it reserves each reaction (`react`), so that they act one after the other. **The owner's manual play counts as a sitting** by the real person and pushes the next simulated one back by its gap, as the turn actor's turn by hand did, now across every bot of the person. **How attention learns of it: it asks its players** when a sitting is due (and once every node has started, `ready`), each answering from its parser (`ready`'s last sends marked `byHand`, any command, D132); the newest, if newer than its last sitting, is a sitting of the person's own, logged `seen`, and nothing plays then. Chosen because the moment that matters is the one before a sitting starts, and attention is the one deciding it: players that reported (an action on attention) would have to watch their parser between sittings, when they sleep, or would learn of it only at the sitting itself, too late and each racing the others; attention reading the parsers itself would need an edge to each parser, repeating every player's. **The `player`**, one node per bot, replaces `turn-actor` (deleted, with `schedule.ts`'s per-actor schedule): bound to its bot's private chat (chat-out, `single`, D97), its parser (an interface contract, `state.ready`, `actions.sent`, required: drift on it stops the player, D64) and its person (`attention`, required). Its config is `commands`, the commands it plays in order, each with a policy: when ready (`{ command }`), or only while another is held (`{ command, whileHeld }`: a reset only while the turn rests). Given a sitting, it plays each that is ready, allowed, and not held back by its outbox (`held`, D98, the safety net), one at a time, each after the person's reaction (a glance, then the answer read), waiting for the answer its parser reads after a live send (up to two minutes) and looking again, so that an unlock announced in an answer, or a reset, is taken in the same sitting; a command already sent in the sitting goes again only if it became ready again since (its `since`), so a dry run, or an answer that holds nothing, plays it once; at most 20 sends a sitting, a guard against two commands that reset each other. Then it sleeps until the next sitting: **no schedule of its own**. Kept: its widget and page (D112: its next play, now its next step or its person's next sitting, on its card; **Plays**, with its chat, commands, last and next), its summary (D92: its commands sent, by command), its steps published (`player.step`), its stop on drift (D64), its dry-run edges (a command logged once a sitting), the instance's off and on, its safety stop; the sitting it is in and its next step (`play`) kept across a restart. **No migration** (D110's practice): the owner deletes the turn nodes before upgrading and adds an `attention` node and one player per bot. Proven on the dev kit with an invented game (`test/quest-clone.ts`): turns come in sittings; a chest a turn's answer announces is opened in that sitting; a coffee that resets the turn gives an extra turn in it; a daily command waits for the first sitting after its day; nights are off; sittings are forgotten now and then; the owner's play by hand puts the next sitting back; a dry run sends nothing; drift stops the player. Rejected: a schedule per player beside attention (independent clocks again, the problem); attention sending the commands itself (it would need each game's chat, parser and policies: one node per bot keeps D97's one chat and the per-bot dry run); the turn actor kept beside the player (two ways to play a turn); a sitting per player, its start drawn by attention but played independently (no bursts across bots, and the players' reactions would collide); polling the parser's answer through the outbox's `await enqueue` (its pairing is in memory and lost on a restart, while the parser's `ready` is kept) (bot-os-api.md §2.1, §2.3, §4.4, §4.17, §5) | D137 | **A player's commands, a checklist of its parser's** (amended by D141; amends D132, D134; P11, P17, D96, D97, D98): a player's `commands` were a list of objects the editor drew as raw JSON, so the owner typed its game's command names from memory, and each `whileHeld` restated what the parser's mechanics already said (a reset clears the turn's rest, so it is played only while the turn rests). **Now the parser publishes its game's commands**: its manifest's `botCommands`, the turn commands first (`{ command, turn: true }`), then the spec's others in its order, each with its mechanics, written by `turnParserPlugin` from its spec alone (the grammars in other modules get it without a change), so the editor knows them without the node running; carried into the plugin's view (`PluginView.botCommands`), and offered at run time by its read `state.commands`. **A new mechanic, `interactive: true`**: a command that needs the person to answer or choose (a minigame, a shop), which a player cannot play blindly; a fact only, the parser tracks it as any other. **The player's policy is derived**: a turn, whenever ready (the bot's rest over); a command whose success clears another's hold, only while that other is held (cooling down); any other, whenever ready. Its config's `commands` became optional: **unset, every command its parser declares but an interactive one, in its order**, read through its parser at its start; set, the explicit list, in its order, each entry `{ command, whileHeld?, whenReady? }`, `whileHeld` and `whenReady` overrides of the derived policy (not both). An explicit list keeps working, but an entry without `whileHeld` now takes its mechanics' policy (a reset listed bare is played only while what it clears is held; `whenReady: true` says otherwise), and an empty list plays nothing. **The editor draws it as a checklist** (`configPlays: { key, input, output }` in the player's manifest, read by the editor rather than its plugin's id): a row per command of the parser its `parser` edge binds, in the parser's order, a box (every one but an interactive one by default; left as the defaults, the config names no commands, and follows its parser as its game grows), a sentence composed from the mechanics and the policy in force saying what it will do (“a turn: played whenever the bot's rest is over”, “played if /play is cooling down; ends its cool-down”, “activated by “A chest appears!”, for 30 minutes: played while active”, “played whenever ready, then cooling down for 24 hours”, “needs you to answer: not played by default”), and its policy to pick, whenever ready or if another command is cooling down; without a parser edge, or with a parser that declares none, the list is typed as JSON, as it can be under **Edit as JSON**. **Its chat edge follows**: each change of the draft sets the `commands` of its chat-out edge to those it plays (`followPlays`), the edge's panel showing them rather than a list to keep in step. Rejected: the commands on the parser's interface output port (its view is derived from its members, and the editor reads a node's view anyway); the player's plugin id known to the editor (a declaration names the key, the parser's input and the chat output, as `configChats` does); the defaults written into the config when the node is added (they would go stale as the game adds a command); drag-to-reorder (the parser's order is its game's, and the policy, not the order, says when a reset goes) | D138 | **Two behaviours of `attention`: its own schedule, and following the owner's play** (amends D133, D134; P6, P10, P11, P17, D96, D97, D127, D132): for some games the owner plays by hand at the keyboard and wants the bot to type for them while they are there (a command they would miss, a reset and the turn it frees), never on a schedule of its own: the owner is present and paying attention, the bot only types for them. **Two booleans, at the top of its config, each on its own:** `scheduled` (default `true`), today's sittings planned from its schedule; off, it plans none (and drops one kept from before), the schedule's fields (gaps, skip chance, wake and bedtime, jitter, wake delay, time zone) are hidden in the editor (`shownWhen`, D127) and checked only while it is on, its reaction kept. `followsMyPlay` (default `false`): **any message the owner sends** (a command or not) in the chats it listens to starts a sitting `followDelayS` later (3 seconds by default, so that the owner's own typing wins a race), every player at once, as any sitting. **How it listens:** a `listen` key, the chats, picked in the editor among the chats of its `listen` input's account (`configChats: [{ key: 'listen', input: 'listen' }]`, written on that edge's `reads`, D96, D97), as the reactor's `in` is; the input, a chat-in of network `telegram` (as a player's chat-out declares), so from the owner's own account (`telegram-user`), exists only while `followsMyPlay` is on (`when`, as the reactor's `chat`; **`when` now takes a key set to `false` as not set**, a switch off, in the core and the editor alike), and is then required, so that the editor draws the port, and the picker has the edge's account to pick from, as soon as the box is ticked. Chosen because it is the codebase's existing way for a node to hear chosen chats of an account: the picker and the edge kept in step by the editor, and turning `followsMyPlay` off takes `listen` away (D127), the port and its edge's requirement with it. It hears the owner's own messages (`own`, or sent as the account's name) live, and only those in a chat `listen` names, whatever the edge reads. **It listens through the owner's own account:** only there is a message the owner's own; a bot's account (`telegram-bot`, network `telegram-bot`) never hears one, so the check refuses its edge, and the editor binds it to nothing but a Telegram user connector. The editor's wiring of a node just added (D135) does not reach it: the port is off then (`followsMyPlay` defaults to `false`), and ticking the box later wires nothing, so the owner draws its edge. (Amended: the input first declared no network, so the editor offered a bot connector, and a `listen` wired to it counted no message, silently.) The config refuses `followsMyPlay` without `listen`, and `listen` without it. **A sitting in progress** (a player still in it: `AttentionPlayer.inSitting`) starts no second: its players in it look again (`again`), and a message while one is pending starts no other. **A sitting that follows counts as the owner's own** (its last, `byHand`), so while `scheduled` the next planned one still comes a full gap after the owner's play. **The answer to the owner's send:** a sitting that follows (`Sitting.follow`), or one the owner wrote during, has its player first wait, as after its own sends (up to two minutes), for the answer to the owner's last send by hand its parser has read none to (`state.ready`'s `sent.byHand` and `answer`), so that a command that answer unlocks, or a turn it holds, is known; then it plays its whole checklist, the turn included, with no new policy. **Both on** is allowed (scheduled sittings, and one more for each burst of the owner's play); **both off** is allowed too, and the check warns that it never plays, through a new generic manifest key, `warns` (a function of the node's config returning warnings, which refuse nothing). Its `status` says its behaviours (`mode`), and its next sitting, not scheduled, reads `follows your play` (or `never: …`), on its card too (an `until` widget shows a string that is no time as it is), the player's next play the same; the summary counts the sittings that followed apart (`3 sittings (1 following you)`). Rejected: a per-command policy for a follow sitting (the checklist already says what it plays); following only commands (the owner's chat text says as well that they are there); a separate "follow" node (one person, one place for when they sit down); an error for both off (a node parked off is a fine state, worth a warning) (bot-os-api.md §2, §5) | D139 | **A player's chat, its bot's or a group's; a command bare or addressed; one bare send, every bot's turn** (amended by D140, D142; amends D97, D134, D137, D138; P3, P11, P17, D64, D98, D129, they would rather the bot played too. **The chat is a choice on the edge**, as D97 made it: a player's chat-out still names exactly one chat, now its bot's `@username` or a group's id (`-100…`, pattern `^(@\w{4,}                     | -\d+)$`), which the editor's chat picker already offered (every chat of the account); its parser's edge must read that group, as it does to count the owner's group turns (D129), so its readiness keeps working. **A command's form, per command, in the checklist** (superseded by D140: the form is chosen at each send, by reach, among those an entry's `forms`allows;`addressed: true`is read as its one addressed form)**:** an entry's`addressed: true`sends it as`/play@QuestBot`, which only that bot takes; unset, bare (`/play`), which in a group every bot that sees it takes (one that is an admin, or without privacy mode), so one send plays them all. The bot's name is the parser's: its manifest's new `botUsername`(written from its spec's`bot`, carried into its view) for the editor, its new read `state.bot`for the player (a member of its contract). The checklist offers the form (a second select, "bare: /play" or "addressed: /play@QuestBot") where the edge sends to a group, or for a command addressed already, and says it in the command's sentence ("sent as /play@QuestBot, which only @QuestBot takes"; "sent bare, which every bot in the group that sees it takes"), with a note of what bare means in a group; not in its bot's private chat, where bare is all it needs. The edge's`commands` follow the form (`followPlays`writes`/play@QuestBot`), since the outbox's reach compares a command's first word as sent; and the parser's answers (D98) name each of its commands bare and addressed to its bot, so that the outbox holds back, and pairs answers to, either form. Defaults stay bare: what a player sent before is unchanged. **One bare send, every bot's turn:** a bare `/play` one player sends in the group is each bot's turn there, but each player told only its own parser (`actions.sent`), and the owner's account never hears its own API sends back. **Chosen: the players sharing an attention hear each other's sends** (moved by D140: the players of one account hand sends off to each other, through the player plugin's own registry; `AttentionHandle.sent`and`AttentionPlayer.heard` are gone)**.** A player tells its person each command it sent live (`AttentionHandle.sent({ chat, text, id, t })`), which tells every other of its players (`AttentionPlayer.heard`), each telling its own parser; the parser now counts a send it is told of (its player's or another's, `byHand: false`) only if it reaches its bot: the command bare or addressed to it (`commandOf`), in its bot's private chat or a chat its edge reads (`ConnectorHandle.reads()`, new, the chats a handle's edge reads), so another bot's private chat or command never counts; it then matches its bot's reply to that message as to its own player's. A player that heard a send during its sitting waits at its next look for the answer to the last unanswered send its parser knows of (up to two minutes, as D138's wait for the owner's, now for any send), so that it never sends its own over a turn just taken; if its bot never answers (it did not see the bare command), it plays after the wait. Why there: attention already joins the players of one person, who share their sittings and reactions (D133, D134), and players of one account are the ones whose sends the account never echoes; it needs no new edge and changes no connector or core delivery. Rejected: the connector echoing the account's own sends to its readers, marked own (every reader of own messages would need to tell a bot's send from the owner's: attention following the owner would follow its own players, D138, and a parser would count them by hand); a player's send told to every parser reading the group by the core (a new core path from an outbox to other nodes' contracts). Its limit: two attentions on one account do not hear each other's players, a sitting's relay is in memory (a parser keeps what it was told), and two players acting within one send's delivery could still both send (their reactions are reserved one after the other, D134). **The owner's bare command by hand in the group** already counted for every parser reading it (D129), by hand; following it (D138), each player waits for its answer, then finds its turn held. Proven end to end on the dev kit (`packages/turns/src/group-play.test.ts`): two parsers, two players, one attention, a bare turn sent once in the group, both bots answering, both turns held, no second send; addressed, one send each; the owner's bare turn by hand followed, none sent. **Not done (the nice-to-haves):** hiding the bare form in a group where the bot is not an admin needs the owner's account to ask Telegram for that bot's rights in that group (a new connector query and an editor route); not built, the checklist shows both forms with the note instead. The addressed form is hidden in the bot's private chat (bot-os-api.md §2, §4.5, §4.16, §5) |
| D140 | **One command, its aliases; each send as the form of widest reach, chosen with the group settled** (amended by D141, D142; amends D132, D137, D139; P3, P11, P17, D70, D97, D98, D133, D134, D138): a bot takes one command by several names (a turn by `/play` and `/quest`, a boost by `/boost` and `/b`), but each name was a command of its own, a `botCommands` row and a checklist row each, and a grammar declared `/boost` and `/b` as two commands with the same mechanics. And in a group the player could not choose the right form: a bare `/play` reaches every bot that declares `/play`, `/quest` or `/play@LoreBot` only @LoreBot; when @LoreBot's boost ends its turn's rest while the others still rest (or one bot's rest differs, doubled after a defeat), a bare `/play` makes the others answer "too soon". **A. One command, its aliases.** A spec's other command declares its `aliases` (`commands: { "/boost": { aliases: ["/b"], ... } }`); `turnCommands` keeps its shape, read as one turn whose first entry is its name and the rest its aliases (`["/play", "/quest"]`: one turn, not two sharing a rest; a grammar that listed several turn commands builds unchanged and gets one row). Any alias, bare or addressed to its bot, sent by hand, told by a player or answered, is its command: one state, one readiness (`state.ready` keyed by names), named by its name everywhere (`BotMessage.command`, `<id>.answer`'s `command`; a send kept before under an alias's name is read as its command's); an effect, an unlock or a reading's `unlocks` may name a command by an alias, resolved (`declaredCommands` writes the name). The manifest's `botCommands` gives each command once, `{ command, aliases?, turn?, ... }`, aliases in their declared order; a name or an alias names one command only (the spec and the manifest refuse it twice, any case); addressed forms are generated, never declared. Its answers (D98) and an effect's `holds` name every form, each name bare and addressed, so that the outbox holds back and pairs each. **B. The checklist and the config.** One row per command; its forms listed, every name bare, then, in a group, every name addressed, each in the parser's order (no addressed form in its bot's private chat, as D139, but one an entry allows already), each with its tick, all ticked by default; an unticked form is never sent, and the last one ticked cannot be unticked (pinning one form). The entry is `{ command, whileHeld?, whenReady?, forms? }`, `forms` the allowed forms in order, unset meaning every one, `command` and `whileHeld` taking an alias too; D139's `addressed: true` is read as `forms: ["<its command, as the entry spells it>@<bot>"]` (by the player and the editor, which writes `forms` back), so a graph saved under D139 keeps its behaviour and its edge's allowed form. The chat edge's `commands` follow the forms allowed (`followPlays`), and each row's sentence says how the form is chosen ("sent as the form that plays the most ready turns at once"; one form: "sent as /play@LoreBot, which only @LoreBot takes"). **C. The form, by reach, in a group by chat output.** The players whose chat-out sends to the same chat from the same account are a group, found through a registry of the player plugin's (`ChatGroups`, `chat-group.ts`, one per `playerPlugin()` registration, in memory, each player joining at its start under its outbox's `account` and its chat, leaving when its instance stops; a node stopped by D64 keeps its instance and stays in, playing nothing, so the bare form is not allowed over its bot, while one shut down, disabled or made inactive, leaves, its bot then out of the reach as one with no player). The reach of a form in that chat is the group's players whose parser takes it (bare `/x`, every bot declaring the name `/x`; `/x@Bot`, Bot's alone), each with its own command it is. **A form is allowed** only if every player it reaches would play that command now: its own attention has it in a sitting (a bot on another schedule is not played unless its attention allows it now), the command ticked and its policy allowing it, ready by its parser (and not sent in the sitting unless ready again), not covered by another's claim, and the form one its config allows and its outbox does not hold back. **The pick:** among its forms allowed, the widest reach; on a tie the first in order (its entry's `forms` in their order, else every name bare in the parser's declaration order, then every name addressed in the same order): a bot's own bare alias (`/quest`) goes before an addressed form (`/play@LoreBot`) when only that bot is ready, the shared bare name still winning by reach whenever it plays several turns, and the parser's order (full names before abbreviations) sets the preference among bare aliases; nothing else is hard-coded, a grammar or the owner orders them. None allowed, the command waits (its only bare form reaching a bot that would not play, and its addressed forms unticked). **The hand-off moves to the account** (amends D139): a live send is told to every other player of the same account, whatever its chat, each telling its parser, which counts it if it reaches its bot (D139's rule), so that a bot played in private whose parser also reads the group still learns of a bare send there; those it reached wait for their bot's answer and do not send over it. Attention no longer relays sends (`AttentionHandle.sent`, `AttentionPlayer.heard` removed): it joined players of one person, who may sit on two accounts, whose sends do not play each other's turns. **D. Settling before choosing.** Bots answer a second or more apart, and rests end seconds apart; before picking a command's form, a player waits while a player its widest form reaches (other than itself) has a send its parser has read no answer to, younger than the answer window (looking again every 5 s), or will have its command ready within `settleS` seconds (a new player config key, 10 by default; waiting until then, so that one bare send covers it); at most the answer window (two minutes) from the first wait (`settling`, kept with the sitting), then it picks with what it knows. A player with nothing ready but a command of its own due within `settleS` stays in its sitting until then, rather than leave it (so that a bot whose rest ends in a few seconds is still in a sitting when the other picks). Then it picks and claims at once, synchronously in the tick of its send: a claim covers the players its form reaches, each for its command, until its hand-off or two minutes, so two players never send overlapping forms; a covered player looks again 5 s later rather than leave. Proven end to end on the dev kit (`group-play.test.ts`): three bots in one group, two whose turn is `/play` and one whose turn is `/play` with the alias `/quest`; all ready, one bare `/play`, all held, no second send; after a boost ends one bot's rest, its own bare `/quest`, not `/play@LoreBot`; with `/quest` unticked, `/play@LoreBot`; two ready and the third resting, each addressed; a player on another attention not in a sitting, the bare form refused; the third's rest ending 4 s after the first look, one bare send once it ends; the alias sharing its command's state; and the reach and pick (`chat-group.test.ts`) and the checklist's forms (`plays.test.ts`, `plays-field.test.tsx`) on their own. **Decided here on the owner's behalf:** the registry lives in the `playerPlugin()` factory, not at module level (it isolates two cores in one process, as the tests run); the hand-off goes to the whole account, the reach and the claims per chat; `forms` as written keeps its order, the editor writing the parser's; an effect's holds clear every form, the bare ones too, so in a group a bot's reset may lift the outbox's cooldown on a bare name that another bot's rest set: the player's reach, not the outbox, keeps the bare form from going then. **Its limits:** a bot that sees the group but whose player sends elsewhere is not in the reach (it may take a bare send it was not counted for); the registry is in memory (a restart re-forms it as the players start); `settleS` and the window are each player's own, so two players with different `settleS` settle differently. Rejected: the registry module-level (shared between cores in one process); grouping by attention (D139's: two people on one account would not see each other's reach, and one person's players on two accounts would); a fixed preference for unique aliases or for addressed forms (the parser's order and the owner's ticks say it); waiting a fixed delay before every send (the answer and the readiness say when the group has settled) (bot-os-api.md §2, §4.16, §5) | Decided; built | D141 | **Readiness in the state, not the parser** (amended by D142, D165; amends D132, D134, D137, D140; P5, P6, P8, D49, D62, D64, D65, D72, D98, D139; #62): since D132 a turn parser did more than read: it tracked every command's readiness (cooldowns, announced unlocks, resets) and declared the game's mechanics in its spec (`cooldownMin`, `unlock`, `effects`, `interactive`), and the player bound to it for `state.ready`, `state.commands` and `state.bot`. That blurred D72's line between a parser (messages into events) and a state (facts reduced from events), and it showed downstream: a game module wrapped its parser's `ready()` to patch in facts its own state knew, a ban or a resource spent since the bot announced it. **The parser: messages to events.** Its spec gives its bot's **vocabulary** (`BotVocabulary`: `bot`, `turnCommands`, and `commands` each with its `aliases` and, for one the bot announces, `announcedBy`, the pattern that was `unlock.pattern`); it publishes each send it counts (`<id>.sent`: `{ chat, command, byHand, id?, playback? }`, by hand or told through `actions.sent`), each answer it reads (`<id>.turn`, `<id>.answer`: the outcome, the wait the bot states as `retryAt`, the commands the message announces unlocked, `unlocks`, the effects it announces, `effects`, and `answer: { length }` when it answers a send) and a message its grammar leaves that answers a send or announces an unlock (`<id>.reply`); it keeps pairing each send with its answer and its D98 declarations, since only it sees both, and a reset the bot announces still ends the outbox's cooldown (`holds`, from the announced effects: a clear at the message's time, a shortening off the last wait it told). Its interface is `actions.sent` alone: no `rest`, `lastTurn`, `ready`, `commands` or `bot`, and no `botCommands` or `botUsername` in its manifest. **The state: readiness and mechanics.** A reusable reducer, `ReadinessModel` (`packages/turns/src/readiness.ts`), built from the parser's id and vocabulary and the game's **mechanics**, declared on the state's side (`cooldownMin`, `unlock: { forMin? }`, `effects`, `interactive`), reduces those events into a section `readiness` of a state plugin (`StateSpec.readiness`), kept and caught up from the log as every state is (D72): a "too soon" holds a command for its wait; any other answer read is a success (its cooldown, or the bot's wait if longer; its unlock used up; its effects); the turn's hold is the longest rest told. A game's state that knows more **folds it in with no wrapper**: its own reducer sees the parser's events after the section did, and applies the model's pure steps (`hold` under a key, on every command or some, until a time or lifted; `succeed`; `unlock`; `lock`). `readinessPlugin` is the generic state, the readiness alone, for a game with none. Such a state offers the **player's contract** (`READINESS_MEMBERS`: `state.ready`, `state.commands`, `state.bot`, `actions.sent`), declares its bot's commands with their mechanics and its bot's name (`botCommands`, `botUsername`, so D137's checklist reads them from it), and has a second input, `parser`, a contract on its parser (`actions.sent`, by default bound to the node of its parser's id). **The player binds to the state** (its input `state`, `configPlays.input` too): its policies stay derived from the mechanics (D137), its reach and form choice (D140), the follow mode (D138) and the settle rules unchanged on the new contract; drift on the parser stops it through the state, which requires the parser (D64, D65). **Its sends reach the parser through the state:** `actions.sent` on the state hands the send to its parser, which pairs its answer and publishes it as `<id>.sent`, which the state reduces; so the player binds to one node, and nothing of readiness is in memory only. **No compatibility** (the owner recreates the graph): no migration of a parser's kept `rest` or `commands`, nor of a player's `parser` edge; D139's `addressed: true` reader is removed (an entry says `forms`). **Decided here on the owner's behalf:** the vocabulary (names, aliases, the announcement's pattern) is the parser's and handed to the state as the same object; the readiness lives in a section of a state plugin, not a node of its own, so that a game's state folds its facts in its reducer; the state relays the player's sends rather than the player binding twice; the outbox's cooldown stays the bot's word: a mechanic's effect the bot does not announce ends the hold in the state alone, and the outbox lifts it only on what the bot announces (a grammar reads a reset's answer with its `effects`). Rejected: the player bound to both the parser (sends) and the state (readiness), two edges to keep in step; the parser publishing its own readiness as events (the mechanics would stay the parser's); the state setting the outbox's holds (the outbox pairs only what a parser publishes while it reads a message, D98); readiness in a separate node beside a game's state (a ban would cross nodes again) (bot-os-api.md §4.16, §5)
