| D142 | **The state alone decides readiness: no cooldown in the outbox** (amends D98, D132, D139, D140, D141; P5, P6, D72, D73, D93, D107, D134; #63): D98 gave the outbox two jobs, for senders that knew nothing of a game's timing (scripts, reactors, the old turn actor): pairing each send with its answer, and holding a command back while the bot's cooldown lasted (an answer's `retryAt` and the commands it `holds`; D132 added `holdsAtFrom`, the times an effect the bot announces sets). Since D141 the state keeps each command's readiness with the whole game's logic (doubled cooldowns, resets, unlocks, aliases), and the outbox's holds were a second, weaker model fed from the same answers: the two could disagree (a reset declared as a state's mechanic did not lift the outbox's hold, so D141 made a grammar read a reset from the reply as well, for the outbox alone). **The state decides** which commands are available, **the player picks** among them by its config, **the outbox only does delivery hygiene.** **Removed:** the outbox's cooldowns (the holds `Answers` kept per chat and command, and what set them); an answer declaration's `retryAtFrom`, `holds` and `holdsAtFrom` (the schema is strict: a manifest that names one is refused); `CommandAnswer.retryAt`, and `ReadAnswer`'s `holds` and `holdsAt`; a turn parser's `holds` in its `<id>.turn` and `<id>.answer` events, and the waits it told the outbox (`told`, in its store's `parsed`, now ignored); D107's notice), the answers still naming every form of a command (D139, D140), for pairing alone; the account's rate limits, the network's flood waits and each command's interval (`minIntervalS`, D73); | D143 | **Serve first; load the plugins, the modules and the connectors in the background, each isolated** (amends D49, D64, D125; P16, D50, D108; #64): two outages took the whole instance down, the web UI included, for a fault in one part. In 0.1.42 one of the image's plugin packages did not parse under Node's type stripping; the entry point imported every package before it served, so the process exited at start, restarted in a loop, and the UI was unreachable (the modules were already refused one by one, but a node of a refused module's plugin refused the whole saved graph). And with Telegram unreachable, the health answered 503 until the connector connected, so the proxy dropped the container and the UI was a 404. **Now:** the entry point serves first: the control API, the health endpoint and the web UI listen before any plugin package, module or connector is loaded. Then, in the background (`bootstrap`, `packages/core/src/boot.ts`), each of the image's packages is imported on its own, side by side, then the modules (D49), each import given 30 s; a package or module whose import throws (a SyntaxError of the type stripping, a top-level error), does not settle, or exports no plugins is a failure of its own: printed, logged (`core.load`), raised as a `load-failed` notice and listed in `GET /status`'s `boot.failures`. **The nodes of a plugin that did not load are held** out of the graph the core runs, `unloaded`, naming the package or module and its error (which one is read from where each plugin came from at the last start that loaded it), and so are the nodes a required port of which binds one (`inactive`, `needs dice (unloaded)`); the rest of the graph runs. Until the load, the saved graph's nodes are `loading`, and a graph is not checked. A node's `create` and `start`, then its `ready`, are each given 60 s: one that does not settle fails alone (what a late `create` makes is stopped), and the start goes on. A connector connects in the background and retries (as the connectors already did), never in its `start`. An error nothing caught (an unhandled rejection, an uncaught exception) no longer ends the process: it is logged (`core.uncaught`) and raised as an `uncaught` notice, naming the module or package its stack names. **The health** (amends D125) answers 200 as soon as the process serves: `ok` always true, with `phase` (`loading`, `starting`, `started`) and `connected` (every counted connector connected) as detail, never a failure, so a proxy never takes the web UI away; the image's healthcheck's start period is 15 s. **The editor** shows each node `loading`, `failed to load` (with the failures, and for a module where to reinstall or roll it back), its connection (`connecting`, D111), `running` or `stopped`, a banner while the plugins load and one listing what failed, and reads the plugins, the saved graph and the check again as the start moves on. A refused saved graph no longer ends the process either (it never did for a file, D50); a graph given by a wiring that is refused is printed, and the process serves on. Rejected: starting the nodes as each plugin arrives, one by one (the graph is checked and ordered as a whole; the packages and modules load in about a second, side by side); a health that fails on its graph (the UI is how the owner fixes it); restarting a node that failed at its start from the UI without a restart (Apply restarts). | D144 | **A message's edits, opt-in** (amends D62, D66, D98; P5, P6, P11): a bot's menu with buttons (a skills menu, an inventory turned page by page) changes in place: each press makes its bot edit the message, and sends nothing new. | D149 | **A plugin's store keeps files beside its documents** (amends the store, bot-os-api.md §4.2; P6, P8, P11, P15; #66): a store kept JSON documents only, so a plugin that makes or receives files it must keep (pictures an image service painted, sent again later as photos; a document a bot sent) had nowhere durable to put them: base64 in a document bloats it and rewrites it whole at every write, and a share mounted into the container widens what the instance reaches, against P6. **Now `ctx.store.files`:** `write(name, bytes, { type? })`, `read(name)`, `list()` (each file's name, size, media type and when it was written, on the core's clock) and `delete(name)`, names as a document's, under `<instance>/files/`, mode 600, each written atomically as a document is, its type and time kept beside it (`files/.meta/`); in the data volume, backed up and restored with the instance, and reaching nothing outside it. **Limits:** 16 MB a file and 256 MB an instance's files together, by default, set by the deployment (`CoreOptions.fileLimits`; the image's `FILE_MAX_MB` and `FILES_MAX_MB`); a write past them throws with why, so no plugin fills the volume. **Migrations** see the files, on the staged copy, which hard-links them rather than copying them: every write replaces a file by a rename and a delete unlinks it, so the store's own files stay as they were until the commit, and a failed migration leaves them untouched. **The owner** lists a node's files and downloads one (`GET /plugins/<id>/files`, `GET /plugins/<id>/files/<name>`, behind the web UI's login as every `/api/` route), and the node's panel lists them, a raster image shown; a file is served sandboxed (`content-security-policy: default-src 'none'; sandbox`, `nosniff`), inline only as a PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP, else as an attachment, so that what a plugin wrote never runs in the UI's origin. Deleting stays the plugin's. The dev kit's stores keep their files in memory, as their documents. Rejected: leaving the files out of the staged copy (a migration could then not rename or drop one, and the commit would have to move them across); copying them for each migration (they may be large); a file's type and time in a document of the store (one more write that two files' writes would race on); deleting from the UI (the plugin owns its state, P6, and may keep a document about each file) | D150 | **An outbox sends a photo** (amends the outbox, bot-os-api.md §4.6, and D109's answers; P6, P10; #68; amended by D164): a plugin could send a photo only as a command's answer, with no caption, so one that reacts to what it reads (another bot's command in a group) could not post a picture with words under it, in reply. **Now** `send`, `enqueue` and `deliver` take a photo where they take a text (`{ photo, caption?, replyTo? }`: bytes and a file name, or the network's id of one sent before; a caption, plain or Markdown as `format` says; the message it answers), through every check a text runs: the reach, a dry run, the node's state, flood waits, the rate, the connection. **A photo has no first word:** an edge that names its `commands` refuses it unless the edge or its output says `photos: true`; it is no command, so no watchdog, no answer, no command's interval, never coalesced. **Refused before sending:** a caption over `CAPTION_MAX`, Telegram's 1024 characters counted as written, and a connector with no `deliverPhoto` (`irc`). `deliver` and a queued send answer the network's id of the photo (`photo`), to send it again by: `telegram-bot`'s `file_id` (`sendPhoto`), `telegram-user`'s `<id>:<access hash>:<file reference>` (GramJS's `sendFile`). `core.send` logs it by its file name and its caption's length, never its bytes. `Answer.photo` takes a caption the same way. | D151 | **A message's photo, fetched on demand** (amends D82; P6, P9, P17; #69): a plugin could read a message's text and a small text file (D82), but no photo, though a game bot's answer is often a photo whose caption is the text a parser reads, the picture itself information (the room a turn happened in). | D153 | **A core `Media` type, shared by every plugin that passes media** (amends D150, D151, D152; P8, P15; #71): three places passed media as `{ data, mime }`, each declaring it on its own (D150's outbox photo, bytes and a file name; D151's `MessagePhoto` and `PhotoResult`; D152's `AskImage`), each with its own schema, checks and types, and more are coming (a game's state that keeps the pictures of its places and answers them to other plugins). | D154 | **An edge to a port gone from its node is dropped, with a warning** (amends D50, D89, §2.3 of bot-os-api.md; P8, P17; #72): a module upgrade that removes a port from a plugin (an optional input dropped) left the saved graph's edge to it, which the check refused (`node postcard: no input port account`), and a refused saved graph runs no node: every unrelated bot of the instance went down with it, and the editor, which draws edges between ports that exist, had nothing to select and delete, so the only way out was editing `graph.json` by hand. **Now** an edge whose two nodes exist and whose input or output port the node's manifest (its own, for a node whose config declares its ports, D74) declares **under no name at all**, neither as an input nor as an output, is stale: the check leaves it out of the graph it holds and gives a **warning** (D89) in its place, `edge telegram-user.interface → postcard.account dropped: postcard has no input port account` (or `… dropped: <node> has no output port <port>`), located on the node, the port and the edge; the load prints it, raises it as a `warning` notice naming that node (D91), and the editor's check shows it; the rest of the graph checks and runs. | D163 | **A table's list of pictures, one at a time** (amends D157; P6, P16; #82): a `table`'s picture column (`show: 'image'`) shows one picture per cell, so a table of a row per subject, each with many pictures (a player's ads, 10 to 30), could not show them in its row. **Now** a column may say `show: 'carousel'`, its value a list of what an `image` column takes (file names in the node's files, `from: 'files'`, the default; or media, `from: 'media'`); an empty list or none, an empty cell; an item that is no picture, skipped. As the page reads again every five seconds, it keeps the picture it shows: found again in its list by itself, else at its place; and since a row whose content changed is drawn anew (its key is what it holds, #79), the section remembers it by column and by the row's name (its first column's text). The manifest's check refuses a carousel whose path its rows have not, as any column's, or whose schema there is no list. | D164 | **A text or a caption in Telegram HTML the plugin writes** (amends D150 and the outbox's format, bot-os-api.md §4.6; P10): a text or a caption was plain or Markdown, which grammy-switchboard turns into Telegram HTML; Markdown has no underline (`__x__` is bold, as models write it) and no way to escape, so a caption that quotes players' names (any character, ASCII art included) inside an underlined title and blockquotes could not be written. **Now** `TextFormat` is `'markdown' \| 'html'`, through `deliver` (a text and a photo's caption), `Answer.text` and `Answer.photo` and every connector: the plugin writes the HTML and escapes `&`, `<` and `>` in words it did not write with `escapeHtml` (`@megabottron1999/core`, beside `TextFormat`). `telegram-bot`, `telegram-user` and the Telegram commands send it as written with Telegram's HTML parse mode, the Bot API's sends again as the text it shows if Telegram cannot parse it, as grammy-switchboard 0.3.0 does; `irc`, which formats nothing, sends that text (`htmlToPlain`: tags removed, `&lt;`, `&gt;`, `&quot;` and `&amp;` unescaped), and so does the outbox for a text sent without its format (`send`, `enqueue`). An HTML caption's length (`CAPTION_MAX`, `photoRefusal`) is that of the text it shows, as Telegram counts it; a Markdown one's is still counted as written. | D165 | **A reset at set times** (amends D132, D141; P5, D137; #83): the readiness mechanics were all relative to a command's last success (`cooldownMin`, `unlock.forMin`), but some games reset a command at fixed times of day: a shop whose items change at midnight, a reward that comes back at 06:00. A cooldown of a day drifts with whoever used it last (used by hand at 14:00, held until 14:00 the next day, past the reset), and no mechanic at all makes it ready at every sitting. **Now** a command's mechanics may say `resetsAt: { times: ['HH:MM', …], timeZone }`: after a success at `t` it is held until the first of those wall-clock times after `t` in `timeZone` (an IANA name, so a change of the clock moves the instant, not the time), why `waits for its reset`. With a `cooldownMin`, or a wait the bot states, the latest hold wins. `ReadinessModel` checks it at construction (at least one time, each `HH:MM`, a known time zone), declares it with the command (`BotCommand.resetsAt`, `state.commands`), and the editor's checklist says it ("then held until 00:00 (Europe/Rome)"). A game whose state sees other players' uses of a shared command (a shop the same for everyone) counts them with `succeed`, as before. Rejected: a player or an attention node woken at the reset (sittings stay the person's; a faster person is a graph's choice); a cron-like mechanic with days of the week (no game needs one yet) | D167 | **People by their stable id** (amends D62, D109, D159; P5, P6; #80; amended by D168): the shell named people by username throughout: `Inbound.sender` (`''` for a sender without one), a chat-in edge's `senders`. A Telegram user may change their username at any time, or drop it, and another may take it: a module that kept a player by username lost them on a rename and handed their place to whoever took the name. A user's numeric id is the one thing that lasts. **`Inbound.sender` is replaced** by `senderId`, the network's stable id (Telegram's, in the Bot API's decimal form: a user's or a bot's, `-100…` for a chat posting as itself; none on IRC), and `senderUsername` (without `@`, an IRC nick; absent, not `''`, without one); a connector handle gives the account's own id, `selfId()`, beside `self()`. **An edge's `senders` entry is an id or a username**: digits (a leading `-` for a chat) are an id, matched against `senderId`; anything else a username, as before (a Telegram username never starts with a digit); a commands edge's took either already. The editor's picker writes a person's id, shown with their current name; a bot stays named by its username, which never changes. **A people directory:** each Telegram connector keeps everyone it has seen (id, current username, name, bot or not, when last seen), `telegram-user` in its store, `telegram-bot` in memory only, as D100 keeps its groups' members off disk (both in their store since D168), so that a plugin finds a person by id or by a username they had when seen (`person`), and hears a rename (`onRename`): what a module needs to read a bot's text that names people by username, and to move what it keeps from a name to an id. A name never seen is not resolved (the Bot API has no lookup; the user account's is a follow-up, #86). **Exports** give `senderId` from the sender's id where they have it (`user<id>`, `channel<id>`), in the same form. **Breaks, as 0.1.69's release notes say:** `sender` is gone (read `senderId` to key a person, `senderUsername` to show one); no username is `undefined`, not `''`; a hand-made connector adds `selfId()`; a reaction's payload names `senderUsername` and `senderId`, not `sender`; edges' username entries keep matching. Each module that keeps people by username moves them to their id itself, as it meets them (the directory's `person` and `onRename`), or from an export, which gives each sender's id and display name. Rejected: keeping `sender` beside the new fields (a use that keys a person would still compile, and keep keying by name); making `sender` the id (every comparison with a bot's name would compile and silently stop matching); converting graphs' username entries (nothing to convert them with, and a bot's need not change) (bot-os-api.md §2.1, §4.5, §4.15) | D168 | **A bot's people directory on disk** (amends D100, D167; P4, P9; #80): D167 kept `telegram-bot`'s people directory in memory only, since D100 had rejected keeping a bot's group members on disk; so a restart forgot everyone the bot had seen, and a module reading through the bot lost the id behind every username until each person spoke again. The owner's reason for lifting it: what is protected is the disk and the machine it runs on, and a Telegram id or username is not a secret worth keeping off it. **`telegram-bot` keeps its people directory in its store**, as `telegram-user` does (`people`, the latest 5000, written when someone is new or changed or an hour on). | D169 | **When a part is a node of its own** (amends P16, D112; P5, P6, P10, P17, D49, D64, D65, D73, D77, D111, D117, D121, D134, D135, D143, D148, D166; #87; amended by D170): a module's plugins grew by accretion, one node doing ten things or ten nodes for one, with nothing to decide by; and a central node's page could show its satellites only by depending on them, a cycle the check refuses. **Split a part into a node of its own when any of these holds:** it has another function, which its kind shows on the map (D111); it is reused, more than one instance of it could exist (P17), though a person's modes stay config on one `attention` (D134); it is enabled or disabled on its own criteria (P10, D64), its stop cascading only to what requires it (D65); it fails on its own (D143); it is the single writer of a state (P6); it holds another credential (D121, D148); it has its own pace or cost (D73, D77, D117); it parses another protocol, whose drift pauses only its own actors (P5); it offers an interface another module could implement (a contract). **Keep parts together when** the interface between them would be chatty; an update must change two states at once, which no two nodes share; or a node would never be turned off, reused or wired differently, and only clutters the map. **Hand wiring is a cost to weigh, not a veto:** a split that a criterion above justifies is made even when its ports are wired by hand (D135 wires a required port only where one candidate serves it, so duplicates wired differently, the reuse case, never can be); where no criterion applies, a split that would cost hand-wired edges is not made just for finer nodes. **Not a node boundary:** release cadence is a module's (D49, D166), and testability alone is no reason, since a node is tested through its interface either way. **Where none applies, keep the node together.** **A UI is a node too:** a node's full page (D112, D157, D163) is deprecated for view nodes (#87), each of which shows the reads and actions of the nodes on its own input edges, wired explicitly; a node keeps its widget on its card. Rejected: one node per plugin file or per responsibility (the map fills with nodes that never move apart); a node boundary at each module (a module is packaging, D49) (bot-os-api.md §2, Widgets and pages) | D170 | **View nodes, served at `/v/<path>/`** (amends P16, D112, D169; P6, P11, P17, P18, D40, D49, D69, D74, D80, D135, D157, D163; #87; amended by D172, D173, D174, D175): a node's page shows only its own reads, so a module whose central node has satellites could show them there only by depending on them, a cycle the check refuses; and a game wanted a home of its own, not `#/node/<id>`. **A view is a node of its own**, of a new kind, `view`, whose manifest declares `view: { title, selector?, sections }`: each section a page's (D112, D157, D163, the same kinds and checks), naming the interface input it reads (`from`). **Its inputs are its edges, wired explicitly:** interface inputs, by plugin or by contract, the members its sections use (`state.<read>`, `actions.<action>`) added to the input they name, so that an edge binds only to a node that offers them (P6, P17); a view's inputs are optional, so a view starts with none wired and D135 wires none for the owner. **Checked against the bound nodes:** the graph's check refuses a section, or the selector, that the node bound to its input does not answer as that node's own page would be refused (a read, an input, a path, a row action); an input left unbound is checked once bound. **A selector:** one choice on the page, its options a list read of a bound node, kept in the address (`?s=`), which sections take as `'$selector'` in a read's input or a row action's, that key left out of its schema's check. **Served at `/v/<path>/`**, behind the UI's login (D40): the node's `path` in the graph (a node field, as `group` is, D69), else its id; the check refuses two views of one path and a path on a node that is no view. The web server serves the app and the API under the address, so the app's relative addresses hold. **Two sources:** a module ships a view as a plugin whose manifest declares it, so a game's page comes with the game; the image's generic `view` takes the same from its node's config (D74), an edge dropped on it adding an input (D80), for the owner's own pages. **Neighbour links:** a view names the nodes it shows, each a link to it in the editor (`#/graph/<id>`); a view node's panel opens its page; every node's panel lists the views that show it. **Its layout** (0.1.72, #87's phase 2; docs/views.md, a cookbook with an example of each): a section is a leaf, which shows a value, or a layout, which holds sections: `tabs` (one level; each its title's slug in the address, `?tab=`, no two alike; only the open tab read), `grid` (`columns`) and `card`. New leaves: `stat`, one value large; `gallery`, a list's items as cards of pictures; `form`, several fields sent at once, an action's input preset from a read or the node's live settings. A table may be searched, sorted and paged, and scrolls sideways in its card. **One word each:** `show` is the kind of a section and nothing else; `format` how a value is drawn (`number`, `percent`, `datetime`, `relative`, `badge` coloured by `tones`, `tags`, `image`, `carousel`); `from` an input, and a picture's `source` (`files` or `media`) where its file is: phase 1's `show` and `from` on a picture column are read as `format` and `source`. **A drawer** (`detail`, on a table or a gallery): a row's fields, actions and sections read with its values (`'$row.<path>'`), at the side of the page, the whole screen on a phone; its row in the address (`?row=`, its `key`, `id` by default), so that a link, one in the owner's chat among them (P18), opens it; one leaf with a drawer a tab. **Every leaf's state:** loading, empty (its `empty`, else `Nothing yet`), or its read's error in its own card, naming the input and the read; an action says it is busy, then its answer or why not, and the leaves of its node are read again. **Checked as written** in the manifest (layout, slugs, a format's options) and against the bound nodes in the graph (each format against its value's type, keys, search and sort paths, a drawer's row paths, a form's action, fields, preset and settings), each error naming its path into the manifest; an unknown `show` lists the kinds there are. **Not yet** (#87's later phases): pushed changes in place of the page's five-second reads (the reads are keyed by node, read and input for it), charts, theme tokens, a sandboxed frame; node pages keep working, deprecated (D169), and their tables take a table's search, sort, paging, formats and a drawer of fields and actions too. Rejected for the layout: a selector per tab (one per page until a view needs more); nested tabs (an address of one tab, and a page an owner can read); a drawer within a drawer. Rejected: a view's inputs required (a view of five nodes inactive while one is off, and D135 guessing its edges); the path in the plugin's config (a plugin cannot know its node's id, and two nodes of one view plugin would share it); a route of its own for a view's definition (`GET /graph/view` already carries the graph and the bound nodes' interfaces) (bot-os-api.md §2, Views, §2.3) | D171 | **Levels for the owner's notices, and a daily digest** (amends D91, D92, D94; P5, P10, P16, P18, D56, D95, D97, D109; #90): `owner-notice` told every notice at its kind's pace and a summary every hour, so a quiet bot still wrote: 117 messages in three days on one deployment (65 summaries, 51 start notices, 1 drift), and the one that mattered was lost among them. **Every notice has a level**, `debug`, `info`, `warning` or `error`: the shell's kinds have theirs (`error` for `failed`, `stalled`, `cascade`, `uncaught`, `load-failed`, `graph-refused`; `warning` for `drift`, `unreachable`, `backoff`, `unanswered`, `refused`, `warning`; `debug` for `coalesced`), a plugin gives its own (`ctx.notice` and `ctx.notify` take `{ level }`, optional, so no plugin changes; a `notify` is a `warning`), and `core.notice` records it. A summary line has one too: a bare text is `info`, and the core's counts of sends and notices and the shell's activity counts are `debug` (`activity()`). **Levels decide only what is sent**: everything is recorded and listed in the node's view, every level. `owner-notice` sends at once what is at or above `level` (`warning`), keeps for **a digest** what is at or above `digest.level` (`info`), and drops the rest; the digest goes once a day at `at` in `timeZone` (`09:00`, `UTC` by default), or every `everyMin`, **and not at all when nothing qualifies**; it replaces the hourly summary. The start notice is `info`, in the digest (`Started 3 times, last: …`), unless an enabled node failed to start, then `error`, at once. **Per node:** `sources` in the config, and the owner's commands `/notices` (the levels, the overrides with their end, the next digest), `/verbose <node> [level] [for <duration>]` (replying with the exact end in `timeZone`) and `/quiet <node>`, served by a commands edge to the owner's chat as any plugin command (D109). **The overrides are kept in the node's store** (`overrides`), not its settings: a setting is a number, a flag, a text or a list of texts, and an override is a level and an end; a store document survives a restart and is the node's own. A command's override wins over `sources`; one past its end is removed and the digest says `quest-state back to warning`. While a node is told below `digest.level`, every `verboseEveryMin` (60) it sends that node's summary lines alone, none when empty, so `/verbose` shows its activity without the rest of the graph. The digest keeps 500 notices in the store and then says `And N older notices not kept`, so a flood cannot grow the store. **A saved graph** has `summaryEveryMin`, deprecated: `60`, the default 0.1.72 wrote into every saved node, counts as unset (so every deployment moves to the daily digest); another number becomes `digest.everyMin`, the owner's own cadence kept; `0` turns the digest off. Nothing is rewritten in the file: the old key stays and is read each time the node starts, until the owner removes it; a `digest.everyMin` the owner sets wins over it, and a `0` keeps the digest off whatever `digest.enabled` says. **What changes for the owner:** a coalesced send is no longer told (`debug`), and the digest has no counts of sends and notices unless its level is lowered to `debug`. Rejected: levels per kind in the config (the per-node override covers the case that came up, a node being debugged, and a kind's level is the plugin's to know); a quiet-hours window (the digest's hour does it for what can wait, and what cannot should wake the owner); overrides as settings (no objects there, and a setting changed from a chat would bypass the editor's save) (bot-os-api.md §4.16, §4.17, §5) | D172 | **No poll from a hidden tab, none twice at once, and the reads in Costs** (amends D77, D112, D170; P11, P16, D111; amended by D173): a module's page asked each of its reads every five seconds (D112, D170) and the editor `GET /status` every five, whether anyone looked or not: with pages open on two machines, hidden tabs included, the core served about 1,060 page requests in five minutes, each read waiting 2 to 3.5 s on its main thread, and a slow answer was asked again before it came. **While `document.visibilityState` is `hidden`, nothing polls**: a node's page, a view, the editor's status and its other loads, and the panels' state and queue; when the tab shows again each asks once at once, then its cadence resumes (`poll` in `hooks.ts`). **No read is asked while its last ask is unanswered**; an ask meanwhile (an action ran) is made once the answer comes. A ticking `until` keeps ticking: it costs no request. **A view asks only what is on screen**: the reads outside its tabs, the tabs' counts, and the open tab's, its open drawer included; a tab switched to asks its reads at once, an older answer kept or not, then joins the cadence. **The reads are counted in Costs**: the control API times each read it serves (`GET /plugins/<id>/state/<read>`) with its answer's serialization and counts its bytes, per node, in its `cost` (`reads: { calls, ms, maxMs, bytes }`), and the editor's Costs adds their time to the node's cost and shows them in a column, so that a view's weight on its node is seen. Rejected: caching a module's reads in the core (the owner declined it: a read's answer is the node's to give, and the polls dropped are most of the load); a slower cadence (a page shown wants its five seconds) (bot-os-api.md §2, Widgets and pages, Views, §4.11; views.md) | D173 | **A view's live updates: changes pushed, reads asked by node** (amends D170, D172; P5, P6, P11, P16, P18, D50, D73, D77, D149; #87 phase 3): a view asked every read on screen every five seconds (D170, D172), changed or not, one request each. **The core tells what changed, not what it is:** a node is touched where the core already sees it change, so that no plugin has to: a write to its store (a document put or removed, a file written or deleted, the core's own documents in its namespace included, its timers among them: one choke point, the store's `changed`), an event it publishes, a change of its state or of a setting of its; and `ctx.changed()`, for a plugin whose reads change without any of those (a status held in memory). The touches are **coalesced over half a second** (`CHANGE_COALESCE_MS`), then **propagated along interface edges** to every node that reads the one touched, however far (a view of donations hears a change of the game state donations reads): the view's input edges already say what it shows, so no new edge is needed. **One stream per open view**, `GET /changes?nodes=<its bound nodes>` (server-sent events, through the UI's login like any route, a comment every 25 s so that no proxy closes it idle), telling `{ nodes }`; the page asks again only the reads on screen of those nodes, in **one batch**, `POST /reads` (at most 200, each counted in its node's `cost.reads` as D172's reads are). **Page Visibility:** the stream is closed while the tab is hidden; when it shows again it opens and every read on screen is asked once; a stream that broke and opened again does the same, since it missed what changed meanwhile. **A safety refresh** asks every read on screen every `SAFETY_REFRESH_MS` (two minutes; one constant in `packages/web/src/ui/view/live.ts`, the owner's to change), for what the core cannot see. Nothing is kept for a listener that is not there: the stream is a hint to ask, never the data. A time shown as `in 5 minutes` ticks in the browser. **What stays a poll:** the editor's `GET /status` (every five seconds while its tab is visible, D172), because what it shows changes mostly without a touch (each node's cost, its handlers' time, its connection), it is one request for the whole map rather than one per read, and the editor is a work tool open while the owner works on the graph; a deprecated node page (D112), which goes with `page` (#87 phase 7); and the panels' state and queue. Rejected: pushing the reads' answers on the stream (a read is the node's to answer when asked, and most changes would push what nobody shows); a stream per node (a view of six nodes would hold six connections); WebSockets (a one-way hint needs none, and server-sent events pass the login and the proxies as any GET) (bot-os-api.md §2, Views, §4, §4.11; views.md) | D174 | **Charts in a view and in the owner's chat, by Observable Plot** (amends D49, D52, D170; P11, P16, P18, D153, D171; #87 phase 4, #54): a view showed values, lists and tables, but no trend: a game's donations per day, counted and not, with their value, could only be read row by row. **Two leaves**, typed and checked as every leaf: `chart` (points by `x`, a category or a number) and `timeseries` (by `x`, a time, gathered by `interval`, `minute` to `month`, in `timeZone`, UTC by default as the owner's notices are, D171), each with a `mark` (`bar`, `line`, `area`, `dot`), `y` (a measure, or up to 8, each a series), `series` (a row's value naming its series, renamed by `seriesLabels`), `stack`, `value` (a second measure, in the tooltip) and `height`. The check, against the bound node's read as every leaf's (D170), refuses an `x`, a measure or a `series` its rows have not, a measure that is no number, a time series' `x` that is no time. **Observable Plot**, as #87 recommended: a declarative spec an agent writes well, SVG that takes the page's colours (`currentColor`, `--chart-1` … `--chart-8`, light and dark) and draws on a server too. **One code for both** (`chart.ts`): the points (gathered and reduced, a time series' intervals with none missing, so that an empty day shows) and Plot's options, Plot given to it rather than imported, so that the web UI loads Plot in a chunk of its own, only on a view with a chart, and the server at its first chart. That code is **a package of its own**, `@megabottron1999/chart` (`packages/chart`), which the core and the web UI both import: it imports nothing of the shell and only Plot's types, so that the web UI, which imports nothing of the core but its types (D43), takes none of the core's Node modules into its bundle. For a plugin or a notice to send a chart to the owner's chat (P18, #54). Rejected: uPlot (time series only, themed by hand), ECharts (the largest bundle), Recharts (React only, no server render), as #87 weighed them; a chart read of its own on the node (the view's read | D175 | **A view's look: theme tokens, and a module's scoped stylesheet** (amends D49, D170; P6, P11, P16, D40, D43, D149, D174; #87 phase 5): a view looked as the editor does, and a module that wanted its game's colours had no way short of UI code, which D49 refuses. **Tokens first.** A view's `theme` (the manifest's `view`, or the generic view's config) sets CSS custom properties on its root, each colour for the `light` scheme and the `dark` one (`background`, `surface`, `text`, `muted`, `line`, `accent`, `info`, `success`, `warning`, `danger`, and up to 8 `chart` colours, D174), its `density` (`compact`, `comfortable`, `spacious`, scaling its spacing), its corners' `radius` and its `font` (a named stack of the host's fonts: no font file is fetched). Every view component draws from the `--view-<name>` tokens alone, and the view's body re-binds the shell's own colours to them, so that its buttons, fields and tables follow; one not set is the shell's, so a view with no theme is unchanged. Set through the DOM's style, not an inline sheet. **A stylesheet second**, which a module's view plugin may ship (`stylesheet: 'views/<name>.css'`, no script), parsed by css-tree as the module loads and **refused, the module with it, unless safe**: the shell wraps it in `@scope` of the view's body (`[data-view-body="<node>"]`), which is positioned, its own stacking context and clips what it holds, so that nothing in it reaches the page around; only `@media`, `@supports`, `@container`; properties on an allow-list (what arranges and colours) and custom properties, so that it may set the tokens; no `content`, `opacity`, `visibility`, `transform`, `filter`, `animation`, `display: none`, `position: fixed` or `sticky`, `!important`; a `z-index` from 0 to 10; functions on a list; `url()` only to a picture of the module's beside it (PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP), served by the instance sandboxed; at most 64 KiB. It is served from the instance (`GET /views/<node>/style.css`), linked by the page, never inline: the CSP is as it was. A confirm is the browser's own (`window.confirm`), so no stylesheet can hide or restyle one; with no `content` and text never HTML, a stylesheet cannot write a button's words. Rejected: arbitrary CSS with selectors checked (a selector cannot be proven to stay inside the view, `@scope` can); `@font-face` (a font fetched is a request of the module's choosing, and its files would need serving: later, if a module needs one); a theme in the owner's config of a module's view (the generic view has one; a module's look is the module's); a stylesheet inline in the manifest (the CSP would need `unsafe-inline` for it, and a file is what a module's author edits) (bot-os-api.md §2, Views, §4.11, §6, §7.1; views.md) ## 5. Open questions

- **Cross-game actions.** None is known (P7). Are there any?

## 6. The path

Built so far (0.1.x): the core (the manifest and lifecycle, the store, the scheduler, the bus and
the event log, accounts and connectors, the outbox, drift, settings, secrets, the dev kit, the
owner's controls, ports and the graph), the IRC and Telegram connectors, the turn plugins, the web
UI's admin pages and graph view, the standard services (D52: SVG to PNG, and LLM access through the
`anthropic` connector), and the module loader (D53: `/data/modules/<id>/`, the resolve hook, version
checks, install and rollback), and the graph in the volume with instances apart from nodes (D50:
`/data/graph.json`, its check, save, rollback and restart through the control API, each node's state
in `/data/instances/<instance>/`), reactions (D58: `react()` and the `reactor`), a game's player
state kept from its parsers' events and drawn from its schema (D72: `statePlugin`), a lazy send
queue with cancellation (D73), chats split into reads and sends, left to right (D60), node states
and dry runs on chat-out edges (D64), and the web UI's graph editor (D55: nodes added, wired,
configured, checked, saved and applied in the UI, its nodes grouped and drawn in swimlanes, D69; the
modules' page, which installs several modules at once from a folder, a GitHub link or a link on a
self-hosted Git server, with their sources and updates, D67, D102).

Next, in order:

1. **Agents** (P11, D14, #51) and plugin widgets (P16, #50).
2. **Launch:** the API locked (P13), and a plugin author's guide (#52).

Built ahead of the launch, at the owner's ask (0.1.3): script nodes (D28, D76), their editor (D78)
and their export as a plugin (D79), and what each node costs (D77); then (0.1.5) an edge dropped on
such a node grows its inputs (D80); then (0.1.7) a message's file, its text read by the Telegram
connectors for the parsers (D82), and a state's own events, told live only, history marked (D83);
then (0.1.8) several ports of a kind on a script node, and a port removed with its edges (D84). The
import of an older version's data (D54) was removed in 0.1.10, its migration over (D86). In 0.1.11
the reactor dropped its age window, history being marked (D88). In 0.1.12 the graph's check gained
warnings, which refuse nothing, the first a chat-in edge reading a chat its connector does not
monitor, as its manifest's `monitors` says (D89); in 0.1.13, a chat matched by any of its names, an
id or a `@username`, in the check and at runtime alike (D90). In 0.1.14, the owner's notices and
`owner-notice`, a node that tells them, grouped and paced, through any connector (D91, #40). In
0.1.15, its summary on a cadence, from lines the plugins contribute, and a notice at each start
(D92, #46). In 0.1.16, a send-queue watchdog that stops an actor whose commands go unanswered (D93,
#41). In 0.1.19, a send the network refuses is recorded and told (D95), and every chat is picked in
one chat picker, never typed (D96). In 0.1.20, a fixed chat is named once, on the edge:
`owner-notice` tells every chat its edges name and the turn actor plays in its edge's one chat, the
reactor's pick written on its edge, saved graphs migrated (D97). Then the Admin page's features
moved into the editor, each on its node, the instance's switches on the map's bar, the page left
named History, for the graph's history (D111, #53). Then a node's widget on its card and its page,
declared from its reads (D112, #50). Then a parser's drift reports by its version (D113), and a
restart logged as one record per phase, not one per node (D114). Then a tool in the image that
creates a `telegram-user` session string (D115, #55), then the Telegram connectors' login from their
node, by token, QR code or phone, kept in their store, their secrets a fallback (D116, #11). Then a
model connector's `$` on its node, every call's cost logged by the connector, and its last 24 hours
on its node, by calling node (D117, #27). Then the Telegram connectors' secrets and the session tool
gone, their login from the node the only way in (D118), and a connector's account its node's id,
nothing to type (D119), and whom it is logged in as on its card (D120), a bot or an account one
node's (D121), and their panel reviewed for a first setup (D122). Then a connector's credentials
sealed at rest under `bot_os_key` (D123), and a plugin's sensitive config fields sealed in the
graph's file and hidden from every view of it (D124). Then a config's choice drawn as labelled
radios, with the fields of the choice made alone (D127), and a bot's groups and people, each any or
only these, in place of its one group and its deny list (D128).
